output.headline: Burnham makes the case for closer EU ties and a £10bn boost
output.bodyHtml:
Andy Burnham has promised a “serious dialogue” over Britain’s long-term place in Europe, framing next month’s Brussels summit as a possible first step towards EU membership, as he said the existing relationship “is not good enough”.

The prime minister said Britain must take a “clear-eyed rational look” at its long-term relationship with the bloc to boost economic growth and control immigration, which needed to go beyond Labour’s existing red lines.

The next “reset” summit will take place on 20 November, ending months of uncertainty, with the two sides seeking to sign deals on food and drink, youth mobility and emissions trading, which Burnham hopes could provide a £10bn-a-year boost to the economy.

One EU diplomat said a deal on the three “significant but modest” issues needed to be approved as a test of the UK’s good faith so both sides could get on with the “real reset” in the longer-term relationship.

Sources on both sides believe they will be able to get other issues over the line at the summit next month, suggesting that a food and phytosanitary agreement would have been reached in July if the summit had gone ahead on its original date.

Burnham pledged to raise concerns with his EU counterparts over possible protectionist “Made in Europe” trade rules, after the UK remained braced for a possible row amid industry fears they could lock out UK manufacturers.

Burnham moved to clarify that he did not think Russian interference in the 2016 Brexit campaign had affected the final result, after he raised questions about the legitimacy of the outcome in comments at the weekend.

Downing Street said the prime minister “absolutely” accepted the Brexit referendum result and believed it to be legitimate, while the foreign minister, Stephen Doughty, said it was clear Russia had attempted to interfere but had failed.

In a statement to MPs, the first since the party conference recess, an otherwise confident-sounding Burnham said it would be a “major dereliction of duty” for his government to turn away from exploring closer relations with the EU.

“We should not turn our backs on this opportunity and I hope all sides of this house will get behind the government’s efforts to land a positive outcome,” he said.

“I believe our chances of doing so will be enhanced by being open to a discussion about our relationship with the EU in the longer term. If we are serious about promoting growth, controlling immigration, upholding our values and security, it is a conversation we must have.

“Sticking with the status quo is not good enough for Britain. Worse, it would be a major dereliction of duty to turn away. We need to take a calm, clear-eyed, rational look at the world as it is today to consider what is best for our country.

“Our immediate priority is securing a successful outcome at the summit, and I believe we should then set up a serious dialogue about the different options for our relationship in the long term.”

Burnham denied he was reopening the Brexit debate, insisting he respected the referendum result, but added that he wanted to take a “pragmatic approach” to boost economic growth and improve cooperation on migration.

Burnham rejected suggestions from Kemi Badenoch, the Conservative leader, that he may have been loose with his language, after facing questions over his remarks on a podcast on Sunday that Russia had interfered over Brexit.

“It is a matter of record that Russian actors sought to interfere in the 2019 general election, and we think it is inconceivable that this was the first time,” he said.

Burnham had said on Sunday it was clear that Russia had interfered in the 2016 Brexit referendum after he sought answers when he arrived in No 10. He did not disclose who gave him the assessment, what evidence it was based on or, crucially, whether any interference had affected the result.

In his statement, Burnham told MPs they were right to raise the question of the “loss of immigration control” that came with Brexit, as Labour grapples with continuing public concern over the issue, and suggested Brussels recognised this.

The UK is excluded from Eurodac, a database that holds biometric and ID data to identify asylum seekers and irregular migrants, and exited the Dublin regulation, a legal mechanism to return refugees to the European country through which they had first entered or transited.

But while the prime minister told MPs a return to free movement was “not on the table” in his discussions with the EU, and said he would honour Keir Starmer’s manifesto red lines, he was unable to rule it out for a post-election future.

Issues still to be resolved include a transition period for grains grown in the UK using recently approved fungicides not yet licensed in the EU. This would allow farmers harvesting this year to sell stockpiles next year even with the different regulations.

The thorniest issue remains the youth mobility programme, allowing EU and British citizens under 30 to live, work or study in each other’s countries for up to three years. The two sides are at odds over the overall numbers, as well as the tuition fees students would pay at British universities.

The biggest current risk to the UK of not aligning more fully with the EU is being locked out of the new Made in Europe initiative – aimed primarily at imports from China in strategic sectors such as renewable energy, nuclear and electric cars – which will block British-made components being used in EU supply chains.

But Brussels is, at least, open to discussing the issue, and it may be part of the summit statement – a joint text agreed by both sides. The UK has the support of the Netherlands, Poland and Italy for inclusion in the scheme, but France in particular has posed a stumbling block.

EU sources have insisted there can be no agreement on the issue with the UK at the summit, because the bloc is yet to agree its own position on the proposals. EU lawmakers hope to agree a position on a key proposal, the Industrial Accelerator Act, in December.

Burnham acknowledged that Made in Europe presented “risks” to British manufacturing, perhaps in an attempt to address some concerns inside government that Downing Street hasn’t been prioritising the issue.

He said: “It is important that we get to an arrangement here that works for both the UK and the EU. After all, we’re both trying to deal with the same issue, which is Chinese exports and the damaging effect that is having on our industry.”
output.standfirst: Burnham says next month’s EU summit could unlock £10bn a year in deals, as the UK works through friction with Brussels over new trade rules and he moves to clarify his Russian interference claims.
output.progress: Burnham has pledged to raise concerns over EU trade rules with his counterparts, as both sides work towards a deal at next month's summit.

output.headline: Scrutiny of student 'super app's China-linked servers prompts calls for transparency
output.bodyHtml:
After the Guardian approached ZyMix about its server contract, the company rewrote its privacy policy and removed mention of Tencent (Frankfurt), which the policy had said stored user-generated content and messages. Tencent’s Shenzhen-based parent, Tencent Holdings, was added to a US military blacklist in January 2026 over its alleged affiliation to the People’s Liberation Army.

A new messaging and payment “super app” marketed at British students uses servers owned by a Chinese company that has been put on a US military blacklist for its alleged affiliation to the People’s Liberation Army.

ZyMix, which is being pushed on university campuses as the UK’s first super app designed “for gen Z”, combining chat, payments and community features, has a contract with a German-based subsidiary of Tencent Holdings, a Chinese conglomerate in Shenzhen.

Tencent Holdings was added in January 2026 to the US Department of Defense’s (DoD) list of Chinese military companies, which is formally known as the section 1260H list.

The citation on the DoD list says that the company, which is a gaming and social media conglomerate, is indirectly affiliated to the Chinese People’s Liberation Army.

The blacklist is part of a US attempt to counteract what it regards as Beijing’s efforts to increase its military power by using technology from Chinese firms, universities and research programmes.

The DoD is prohibited from entering into, renewing or extending contracts for goods, services or technology with any entity on the list although wider sanctions are not automatic.

A Tencent spokesperson said: “Tencent’s inclusion on this list is clearly a mistake. We are not a military company or supplier. Unlike sanctions or export controls, this listing has no impact on our business. We will nonetheless work with the Department of Defense to address any misunderstanding.”

China’s footprint in higher education in the UK has become a controversial issue. MI5 recently warned British universities to cut ties with the China General Technology Research Institute.

Related: MI5 China alert will send chill through UK’s cash-strapped universities

The domestic intelligence service claimed it was secretly channelling funding from Beijing’s intelligence apparatus to UK-linked academics to improve the technical espionage capabilities of China’s ministry of state security.

The link between the Chinese-owned infrastructure and ZyMix was initially disclosed in the company’s privacy policy at the time of its launch last week.

The policy now states that users’ personal data is stored and processed primarily in the United Kingdom and the EU, adding that “some of our service providers are located in other countries, including the United States”.

It goes on to say that “auxiliary infrastructure providers, hosted in the EU, receive only encrypted user messages and limited technical data, such as technical statistics, licence validation when the app starts”.

A spokesperson said: “As a newly launched startup, we are updating our privacy notice as we develop our services, including clarifying that Tencent, Twilio and the other providers concerned are used solely for performance testing.”

The spokesperson added: “Our agreement is with Tencent Cloud Europe BV, which we use for auxiliary services, rather than as the provider that stores ZyMix user data. We take our obligations under UK data protection law seriously.”

The new privacy policy invites those who wish to know the identity of their suppliers to request the information from the company.

In response to a request from the Guardian, Tarique Ghaffur, a former assistant commissioner at the Metropolitan police, who described himself as a security consultant for ZyMix, responded.

He said: “We have reviewed your request as against our private privacy [sic] you mentioned. Unfortunately, at the present time for reasons of commercial confidentiality, contractual obligations and legal privileges, we are not able to provide you with the requested information.”

Fraser Sampson, a professor of security and national governance and formerly the UK’s biometrics and surveillance camera commissioner, said he was “sceptical when ‘commercial confidentiality’ arguments are used to duck basic policy questions and amending policy on the fly is never reassuring”.

He added: “When companies ask us for our personal data, they should expect us to ask them where it’s being kept, for what purpose(s) and who they’re going to share it with – and be prepared to answer fully.”

Sam Dunning, the director of the UK-China Transparency NGO, said: “There are serious questions about whether ZyMix have taken due care before launching this product.”

A spokesperson for ZyMix said: “Whilst still in its beta stage, the ZyMix app has been developed to fully comply with all UK data, privacy and financial regulations.”

ZyMix is heavily targeting the university market and is offering £200 to £400 a month to people who agree to be brand ambassadors on campuses. Staff roles have also been advertised in the UK by ZyMix for Mandarin-speaking applicants.

One advert on LinkedIn for the job of operations manager (Mandarin speaking) required “excellent written and verbal communication skills in both English and Mandarin (required for daily communication with the China team)”.

Separately, a distinct company appeared to be recruiting on behalf of ZyMix on WeChat, the Chinese instant messaging service, saying: “The product, R&D, design and testing team is in Greater China, with branch-company bases covering: Taipei / Shenzhen / Guangzhou / Hangzhou / Chengdu / Zhengzhou.”

Ghaffur said that Flicknmix, the UK company that publishes the ZyMix app, “does not have any subsidiaries or branch offices in China. Our aim is to create opportunities within the UK”. A spokesperson for ZyMix described it as “British born”.
output.standfirst: ZyMix removed mentions of Tencent, the Chinese conglomerate linked by the US to the People’s Liberation Army, from its privacy policy after the Guardian asked about its Chinese-owned server contract.
output.progress: Fraser Sampson and the UK-China Transparency NGO are pressing ZyMix for transparency over its Chinese-linked server contract.

output.headline: Polling body demands answers over hidden Farage-linked consultant's role
output.bodyHtml:
The Guardian can reveal that a close adviser to Nigel Farage had an influential role at a national polling company despite not being publicly associated with the firm.

Several sources who have worked at Redfield & Wilton Strategies said Chris Bruni-Lowe, Farage’s private pollster for many years, played an important role in its operations and used it to develop potential campaign strategies.

The firm, founded in 2020, is owned by Bruno Rodrigues, a lawyer. Its main public face was Philip van Scheltinga, a Harvard graduate.

Former employees have now revealed the important role of Bruni-Lowe, who sometimes went by the name “Chris Redfield”, under which quotes were published by the Washington Post newspaper. As the Covid pandemic grew and the UK entered lockdown, the company’s polls received increasing coverage, even while the source of the firm’s polling expertise was unclear.

As well as ordering UK and US voter intention polls, sources said Bruni-Lowe directed research on issues such as council spending, and appeared “obsessed” with producing a dossier which he suggested could be sold to political parties.

Bruni-Lowe’s role at the company will amplify questions about transparency in the polling industry, given his longstanding association with Farage at a time of intense scrutiny over the party’s use of polls to shape its political narrative.

The rules of the British Polling Council do not require pollsters to state any political affiliations, but they have strict guidelines on how they must declare who has commissioned and paid for any polling.

In a statement, Rodrigues, the company’s sole director, said there had never been “an institutional, polling, research, commissioning or financial relationship” between Redfield & Wilton and Reform UK or Farage.

He said Bruni-Lowe had worked as a “consultant” from mid-2020 until late 2022, and returned “voluntarily” in the summer of 2025 to train interns. Rodrigues added that Bruni-Lowe was “an important and highly valued member” of the team.

Sources said Bruni-Lowe, who some employees said had been known as “Chris Redfield”, was heavily involved in the company’s polling operations.

Rodrigues said the surname Redfield was used as an email account convention within the organisation, citing other examples of “Philip Redfield” and “Bruno Redfield”. He said: “It was not a device created specifically for Chris and it did not conceal his identity from people working within the company.”

Nonetheless, the situation was confusing enough that at least one newspaper, the Washington Post, attributed quotes to that name, while notes taken by one former employee during an oral induction in the summer of 2021, and seen by the Guardian, described “boss – Chris Redfield is COO essentially”.

Rodrigues said: “He was never presented to staff as the company’s chief operating officer and staff were never instructed to treat him as such.” He added that Van Scheltinga, as director of research, led the “day-to-day operation”.

The Guardian can also reveal that Dan Jukes, then a senior adviser to Farage, sought to promote Redfield & Wilton’s work in 2020, looking to place exclusive polls in publications including the Guardian, which turned down the offer.

Jukes stepped down as Farage’s chief of staff recently over a scandal in which undercover reporters posed as potential overseas donors to Reform UK. Footage published by Channel 4 News showed the co-founder of polling firm JL Partners, James Johnson, apparently acknowledging that Jukes had commissioned polling funded by an overseas donor.

The polling had appeared in newspapers without any reference to the party, with JL Partners acknowledging “weaknesses” in its procedures.

Jukes denies wrongdoing and Reform UK has said the party itself did not commission the work. On Wednesday, Reform announced that an internal inquiry had cleared the officials of breaking the law. The matter remains under police investigation.

Redfield & Wilton started producing polls in 2020 with little information about the people behind the company. During its publicly active years before it became less visible in late 2024, its voter intention polls frequently appeared in politically influential newsletters from Politico, the Times, and the New Statesman.

Bruni-Lowe ran Farage’s 2015 election campaign, helped test messaging for the formation of the Brexit party and advised on the 2019 local elections campaign, as well as having produced private polling for Farage since at least 2014, apart from during a brief period of working for Rishi Sunak before the 2024 election. In his book on political strategy, he writes of having worked for “organisations and candidates of all political persuasions”.

He is considered to be part of Farage’s inner circle and was close enough to the Reform UK leader to have been present on a trip to party donor Christopher Harborne’s Thai wellness retreat at Christmas in 2022 to mark the crypto billionaire’s 60th birthday.

Other guests photographed at the meeting include Farage’s unpaid aide and convicted fraudster George Cottrell.

In May 2023, Van Scheltinga and Bruni-Lowe were photographed having drinks at a Mayfair restaurant with Farage, Cottrell and Richard Tice, the Reform UK deputy leader.

Rodrigues said: “The existence of personal or social meetings involving individuals associated with the company does not establish a corporate relationship between Redfield & Wilton Strategies and Reform UK.”

While much of Redfield & Wilton’s published polling related to voter intentions in the UK and the US, sources said Bruni-Lowe had its staff develop a “dossier” on local authority performance between autumn 2024 and spring 2025.

One source said he suggested the firm’s work could be sold to political parties, and that Bruni-Lowe appeared “obsessed” with the dossier. Research by employees included freedom of information requests to councils to find expenditure on translation services.

Rodrigues said the FOI project was a “commercial research project” and translation services were just one of “several dozen categories” examined by the company in a project led by Van Scheltinga. He added that none of the research was supplied to Reform or Farage.

The company’s other work, sources said, included polling in Montenegro, Hungary, Hong Kong and the Bahamas, as well as research about attitudes in the UK to gold and cryptocurrencies.

Employees were not always told exactly how their work would be used. According to one former employee, they were told their work on a foreign election would be for the Telegraph, but the polling never appeared in the newspaper. Another said they believed their work on cryptocurrencies was for a client.

One unusual piece of work by the company was an October 2021 submission to an inquiry into central bank digital currencies (CBDCs) carried out by the House of Lords economic affairs committee. The company cited polling it said “was self-funded internally by Redfield & Wilton Strategies Ltd for the purpose of this submission”.

The submission said the scepticism of the British public over the UK government’s capacity for innovation meant “it is strategically important that alternatives to a CBDC from the private sector, including those that are already in use, are also given the opportunity to be developed further”.

According to a person who worked at the company at the time of the submission, “all of the crypto stuff came down from Chris [Bruni-Lowe]”.

One online profile for Rodrigues, a solicitor based in London, refers to him holding a directorship of an “innovative market research firm”. However, according to former employees, he had a limited role in the day-to-day running of Redfield & Wilton. One source said that at a rare in-person meeting Rodrigues was “paraded around on a laptop on a Zoom call”.

Van Scheltinga was frequently quoted giving analysis of the company’s polling and wrote columns for the Times and Telegraph.

Van Scheltinga was the listed contact for the company with the British Polling Council, the trade body for pollsters, but one industry source said he never attended BPC meetings. This led to demands from the BPC for a representative of the group to appear before them: that was ultimately Rodrigues, the nominal director, who maintained “total silence”, according to the industry source.

Bruni-Lowe declined to comment. Van Scheltinga did not respond to requests for comment.
output.standfirst: Former employees of Redfield & Wilton Strategies have revealed that Chris Bruni-Lowe, Farage’s private pollster for many years, held an unpublicised, influential role at the firm, using it to develop potential campaign tactics, sources say.
output.progress: The British Polling Council demanded a representative appear before it after the firm’s contact never attended BPC meetings, though Rodrigues maintained ‘total silence’.

output.headline: IMF sets out global exposure to an AI share market correction
output.bodyHtml:
The International Monetary Fund has set out how an AI share price crash rippling out across global markets could affect world financial stability.

In its twice-yearly Global Financial Stability Report, the IMF highlighted the sky-high valuations for AI companies, along with their increasing debt pile, as one reason why risks in the system are ‘elevated’.

‘The consequences of an AI correction could be global,’ the IMF warned. Aside from the US, Asian markets would be most exposed, while the UK and euro area are potentially more insulated – though their investors with exposure to the US would still be hit.

An AI crash was one of three ‘salient risks’ to stability identified by the IMF, alongside rising government borrowing costs and the threat of a big cyber-attack.

The IMF called this trio of factors ‘plausible near-term catalysts for a sharp tightening of financial conditions and market turmoil’.

The IMF’s analysis underlined the interconnected nature of big AI companies, and the high levels of borrowing being undertaken to fund investment in the sector.

‘Weaker or less durable investment and profitability in AI could trigger a correction in AI-related asset prices, exacerbated by rising leverage, concentrated exposures and circular financing arrangements,’ it said.

Such a reassessment would then ‘sharply reduce investment, trigger equity market corrections, and tighten financial conditions, with global spillovers’.

The ‘magnificent seven’ big tech stocks – Alphabet, Amazon, Apple, Meta, Microsoft, Nvidia and Tesla – account for more than 35 per cent of the S&P 500 share index in the US, up from 12 per cent a decade ago, and their total market capitalisation has increased by more than 50 per cent in the past two years.

Yet the IMF also warned of ‘growing evidence’ that the successful rollout of AI ‘may not require investment on the massive scale being undertaken by “hyperscaler” firms’, and that ‘potential economic gains may not be as large as expected’.

The hyperscalers are the companies building the underlying infrastructure for the AI rollout, including many vast datacentres. They include Amazon Web Services, Google, Meta and Oracle.

The IMF also highlighted the growing leverage, or borrowing, that underpins the current boom and could amplify the effects of a crash.

In particular, it identified soaring debts contracted by the companies themselves, hedge fund investment in the sector, and retail investors borrowing to speculate in AI stocks.

In the event of an AI-led market downturn, ‘these growing sources of leverage heighten the potential for forced selling and surges in equity volatility’, it said.

It also pointed to the prevalence of ‘circular financing’ deals, tying stronger AI companies to weaker partners in the same sector, and potentially exacerbating the impact of a share price correction.

It identified $300bn (£227bn) worth of transactions between hyperscalers and ‘weaker AI firms’ in just the past three years, supplemented by $650bn in debt, in exchange for $1.4tn in future financial commitments.
output.standfirst: The UK and euro area are potentially more insulated than the US and Asia, the IMF says, as it flags AI valuations and debt, rising borrowing costs and cyber-attack exposure as factors that could unsettle markets.

output.headline: Government clears £5bn Send debt, guarantees 90 per cent of debts to March 2026
output.bodyHtml:
The government has already cleared more than £5bn in historic council Send debts, but councils forecast that remaining pressures could become “catastrophic”, with debts reaching a record £10bn over the next 18 months, as a result of rapid growth in demand for special educational needs and disability (Send) support in English schools.

A surge in requests has led authorities to predict they will re-accrue that £5bn figure by April, and double it by 2028.

The recent acceleration in applications for education, health and care plans (EHCPs), which mandate support for conditions such as speech and learning difficulties, autism or ADHD, is thought to partly reflect a rush by parents and schools to secure support before the government’s changes to Send provision take effect.

The prospect of council finances being overwhelmed by schools’ Send spending reflects similar concerns in the NHS and the benefit system over the strain the rising prevalence of mental health and neurodevelopmental conditions has put on public services.

The government-commissioned Fonagy report, published last week, found the increase in these conditions was real and a cause of distress to many who have them, but the resulting demand for support would be unsustainable without introducing new ways to manage the pressure on public services.

Ministers have agreed to pay 90% of English top tier councils’ Send debts accumulated to March 2026, but it is unclear how far future Send debts will be covered. Ministers have previously said future debt support would be “appropriate and proportionate” but that it would “not be unlimited”.

A government spokesperson said: “We inherited a Send system under immense strain, and have always recognised that both deficits and EHCP applications will continue to rise before our reforms are fully rolled out.

“On top of grants to pay off 90% of council deficits, we’re investing billions to make sure every community has easy, early access to specialists like speech and language therapists, and so councils can deliver their tailored local reform plans.

“Fixing the Send system will take time and councils will need further support with deficits, so we will set out the details before March 2028.”

The County Councils Network (CCN), which published the forecasts on Tuesday, said the overspending was not the fault of councils and called on ministers to guarantee future Send debts run up by local authorities, some of whom would be otherwise left effectively bankrupt as a result of meeting their legal duties.

Linden Kemkaran, the CCN’s Send spokesperson, said: “These deficits have not accumulated because councils have chosen to spend recklessly: they are the result of having to meet rapidly growing statutory demand, which has only intensified this year, without funding keeping pace.

“If councils are left carrying billions of pounds of Send debt, it will not just be a problem for local authorities. Taxpayers and local communities will ultimately bear the consequences as councils face impossible choices about how to protect frontline services while managing debts that have accrued through no fault of their own.

She added: “As well as councils absorbing skyrocketing costs, children and young people will face increasingly long waits for support and educational outcomes will continue to flatline. New ministers now need to provide certainty that they will deliver the full package of reforms needed to ensure the system works much better for young people, schools and councils.”

The government’s reforms aim to gradually replace the current system in England with a more inclusive approach of Send support in mainstream schools that in principle obviates the need for an EHCP. However, parents appear to be rushing to secure formal support now to avoid any future uncertainty.

Without a ministerial guarantee to wipe future overspending, councils say they are at risk of bankruptcy when those accumulated debts – currently kept off town hall balance sheets under a special “override” arrangement with the Treasury – go back on to the books in April 2028 when the override is due to expire.

Related: Headteachers threaten strike ballots after losing confidence in Ofsted

The CCN said anything less than a ministerial commitment to pay down 90% of future Send debt would be a “financial catastrophe” for councils – and some authorities would struggle with solvency even if they retained just 10% of their Send debts.

Publicly available internal reports by local authorities show a number are predicting overspends of more than £100m in 2026-27 alone. Hampshire county council is forecasting a £200m deficit for this year. Others include Surrey, East Sussex, Kent, Worcestershire and Norfolk county councils.

The EHCPs are legal documents agreed between local authorities and families in England detailing the support required for children and young people up to the age of 25, allowing access to extra funding or places in special schools.

In January, the number of young people with EHCPs reached 718,000, after a 12.5% increase over the past 12 months. This was the largest year on year increase since the plans were introduced in 2014. An additional 1.3 million young people have identified special needs, according to official data.

Many councils are anticipating annual double digit increases over the next three years, with several now projecting that at the current rates of increase, nearly one in 10 pupils will have an EHCP by 2029.

The Fonagy report said the growth in EHCPs had “substantially outpaced the capacity” of the education system to respond. Of the 105,300 statutory assessments carried out in 2024, 94% resulted in the award of an EHCP.

Owen Mapley, the chief executive of the Chartered Institute of Public Finance and Accountancy, said: “The continued escalation of Send deficits exposes a serious failure to align statutory responsibilities with funding levels. Local government chief financial officers have been calling attention to this disconnect for years as it undermines proper financial management practice.”
output.standfirst: The government has already cleared £5bn of council Send debt and is investing in specialist support, as councils forecast a ‘catastrophic’ shortfall reaching £10bn by 2028.
output.progress: Ministers have cleared £5bn of council Send debt, agreed to fund 90 per cent of debts to March 2026, and are investing in specialist support.

output.headline: Lead researcher calls on doctors to tell patients ‘I believe you’
output.bodyHtml:
Melanie Sloan, the study’s lead author, is calling on doctors to stop assuming patients’ symptoms are psychological, after a study found women with autoimmune conditions are up to 74% more likely than men to be told their symptoms are psychological or psychosomatic, and face much longer waits for a diagnosis and treatment.

Hundreds of millions of people – about one in 10 globally – are affected by autoimmune conditions, which can cause a range of health issues including fatigue, muscle pain and rashes.

But research by the University of Cambridge and University of East Anglia suggests a stark gender divide when it comes to how signs of the conditions are handled by doctors.

Women are more likely to have their conditions wrongly attributed to psychiatric causes, more likely to have symptoms misdiagnosed as psychosomatic, and more likely to experience delays in getting a diagnosis, according to the study.

The lead author, Melanie Sloan, said: “The damage caused to women by these types of misdiagnosis can be very long lasting in terms of trusting doctors and their own self-esteem.”

Sloan, a researcher in the department of public health and primary care at Cambridge and UEA, said some women were forced to wait years before finally getting a diagnosis, causing long delays to treatment for their condition.

Sloan said the findings “highlight that psychological or mental health explanations can be given too soon”.

She added: “This is true for both sexes, but our study suggests that females may be particularly vulnerable to these types of misdiagnoses.

“It is really important that symptoms are not automatically assumed to be psychological and for doctors to just say, ‘I believe you,’ to patients with symptoms that the doctors cannot see.”

The study, published in the Lancet eClinicalMedicine journal, included more than 6,600 people with autoimmune conditions. Most were female and from the UK.

Patients listed their main condition, with almost a quarter of the women having autoimmune thyroid disease, which can cause the gland to become underactive – known as Hashimoto’s disease – or overactive, known as Graves’ disease. Hashimoto’s disease can cause weight gain, hair loss, fatigue and joint pain, while the symptoms of Graves’ disease include bulging eyes, palpitations and weight loss.

One in seven women in the study had systemic lupus, which can cause tiredness, rashes and muscle pain.

Among male patients, rheumatoid arthritis, vasculitis and antiphospholipid syndrome (APS), also known as “sticky blood” syndrome, were the most common conditions.

Researchers found 43% of women reported being told their condition was down to a psychiatric cause compared with a third of men (33%).

A third (34%) of women also reported having symptoms misdiagnosed as psychosomatic – meaning they were triggered or worsened by stress or anxiety – compared with 22% of men.

Overall, after accounting for factors including age, disease group, continent and household finances, researchers said women were 46% more likely to report having received a psychiatric misdiagnosis, and 74% more likely to report a psychosomatic misdiagnosis than men.

Researchers also found women reported much longer periods between the onset of symptoms and receiving a diagnosis, as well as more healthcare consultations. Among men, the most frequently reported time to diagnosis was less than three months. Among women, it was one to two years.

Autoimmune conditions, which happen when the immune system attacks the body by mistake, can be complex to diagnose as they often present with symptoms common in the wider population.

The study team said “broader diagnostic challenges affect both sexes” but “females may face additional disadvantages”.

They added: “Historical biases in medicine may persist, including positioning females as less credible and emotional reporters of symptoms than males.”

Shaista Tayabali, a patient affected by an autoimmune condition who was part of the research team and a co-author of the study, said: “The differences between the sexes in misdiagnoses for people with autoimmune diseases is stark.

“The fact that females reported higher rates of psychiatric and psychosomatic misdiagnoses than males … suggests that historical gender biases remain a challenging aspect of the diagnostic journey.

“Although labels such as hysteria are outdated, and fortunately rarely used nowadays, as women we still often have a harder time having our symptoms believed and therefore addressed accurately.”
output.standfirst: Melanie Sloan, the study’s lead author, calls for doctors to stop assuming symptoms are psychological, as Cambridge research finds women up to 74% more likely than men to be misdiagnosed and wait longer for diagnosis.
output.progress: Lead author Melanie Sloan says doctors should tell patients, ‘I believe you’, instead of assuming symptoms are psychological.

output.headline: Breaking Bad costars celebrate RJ Mitte's legacy as disability advocate
output.bodyHtml:
“It is with profound sadness that we share the tragic passing of beloved actor, philanthropist, and passionate disability rights advocate RJ Mitte,” Mitte’s representatives said in a statement. “Drawing from his own experience living with cerebral palsy, Mitte brought authenticity to the role and built a platform on disability awareness and inclusion.”

Offscreen, Mitte was an outspoken advocate for disability representation in entertainment, and served in various philanthropic roles, including as an ambassador for United Cerebral Palsy and as president of the Mitte Foundation.

Related: RJ Mitte: ‘By 13, I was the main breadwinner for my family. It was scary but necessary’

The Breaking Bad actor RJ Mitte died on Monday aged 34, his representatives confirmed.

Mitte died in Brownsville, Texas. No cause of death was given.

The Brownsville Police Department said no foul play was suspected and the investigation into his death was ongoing. Cameron County justice of the peace, Cyndi Hinojosa told the Associated Press that an autopsy would be performed.

From the age of 15, Mitte played Walter White Jr, the son of Bryan Cranston’s high school chemistry teacher turned drug kingpin, on 56 episodes of the acclaimed AMC show, which is often cited as one of the best television programs of all time.

Mitte had cerebral palsy, a condition he shared with his Breaking Bad character.

In 2015, he spoke to the Guardian about being a disabled actor who plays disabled characters.

“You accept the risks and you accept these will be the parts you play. But it’s all about how you play those parts – you have to show the inner strength that people have.”

Mitte’s costars paid tribute to him after news of his death broke, including Bryan Cranston who wrote a lengthy tribute on Instagram.

“I’m in deep despair as I write this tonight,” Cranston wrote. “RJ Mitte, my sweet son on Breaking Bad has died. I met him when he was only 14 years old when he was cast as Walter White Jr, a part he played with such joy and enthusiasm. Born with cerebral palsy, he never – ever – allowed that challenge to be an excuse for anything. He met the demanding shooting schedule head on with great determination. Always listening to the advice that his TV parents (Anna Gunn and myself) gave him – but being a teenager, sometimes mischievously ignoring the counsel in order to learn the hard way… He was one of the stars of a hit TV show – but still a kid.

“That kid was pretty raw when we started shooting the pilot in February of 2007, but little by little we watched him grow into a really fine actor. He parlayed his experience on the show to be a vocal advocate for performers with disabilities, and was the head of a philanthropic organization with a focus on helping the disabled community. All that promise and potential now is such a loss.”

Cranston said he “thoroughly enjoyed being with him throughout the years on the series, and after the spotlight on Breaking Bad dimmed… I’ll miss you, son.”

Aaron Paul, who played Jesse Pinkman, said in a statement: “I am at a loss. I am heartbroken over this news. RJ, I love you my friend. You will be missed.”

Dean Norris, who played Walt Jr’s uncle Hank Schrader, wrote on social media: “Though RJ didn’t play my TV son, I always looked out for him as a young kid on set. He was a sweetheart of a young man and will be greatly missed. This is so heartbreaking, I can’t believe it. Thinking of him and his family.”

In addition to Breaking Bad, Mitte had roles on several series, including Switched at Birth and The Guardians of Justice. Just days before his death, he was promoting his new movie, Talking to Strangers, billed as a “romantic tragedy”.

Earlier this month, Mitte appeared on the Joe Vulpis Podcast, speaking in depth about his time on Breaking Bad. He noted his character was based on a real-life friend of the show’s creator, Vince Gilligan.

“It really felt real playing this character and getting into the groove with this character,” Mitte said.

Born in 1992, Mitte was raised in Mississippi by adoptive parents. In a 2016 interview with the Guardian, he said he found out he was adopted when he was eight years old.

“My step-brother told me. He’d overheard my mum and my stepdad at the time talking about it, and he threw it in my face. But I didn’t really care. It didn’t seem relevant, because I never once in my life felt unloved or like I was a burden.”

output.headline: Food historian cooks her way through a century of Britain’s seafood recipes
output.bodyHtml:
In days gone by, the UK’s domestic cooks were an adventurous lot when it came to seafood, prepared to dish up anything from an oyster cocktail to whale meat curry.

Ruth Thurstan, from the University of Exeter, has studied more than 1,000 fish and shellfish recipes published in the British version of the lifestyle magazine Good Housekeeping from 1923 to the present, charting how tastes have changed over the last century. Her investigation suggests tastes have become much narrower.

She found that 67 species had been included in recipes over the last 100 years but, since the 1970s, the ‘big five’ – cod, haddock, tuna, salmon and prawns – have dominated, accounting for more than 60 per cent of all mentions. The number of recipes featuring delicacies such as oysters, flatfish and herring have plunged.

Thurstan said: ‘For decades, British cooks have turned to published recipes for inspiration about what to put on the dinner table. I wondered whether these everyday sources could tell us how our relationship with fish has changed over time.’

She said there were three broad phases:

  • Pre-1970s: A diverse mix of species in recipes. No single group ruled but flatfish, herring and oyster were prominent. Recipes emphasised domestic skills, economy and preparing whole fish.

  • The 1970s shift: A decline in diversity of fish species in recipes, with increased focus on the ‘big five’.

  • 1980s-present: ‘Big five’ present in the majority of recipes, with a decline of other species – though not all have vanished entirely.

Recipes from the 1920s and 30s that Thurstan found included oyster cocktail, lobster canapes and halibut steaks in milk. The 1940s – when rationing was in force – featured recipes by the then Ministry of Food explicitly encouraging the consumption of fish and other protein sources – including a recipe for curried whale meat.

In the 1960s, recipes included plaice véronique and chilled prawn soup. Cooks of the 70s were asked to consider rustling up cod roe on toast and tuna soured cream quiche. There was also a sharp increase in recipes mentioning tinned fish.

Recipes in the 1990s featured the likes of herb-crusted salmon and prawn and peanut noodles while more ‘aspirational’ dishes in the 2020s have included golden hasselback salmon, gochujang sticky cod and miso prawn skewers.

‘The results reveal a striking story of change,’ said Thurstan, whose research is conducted at the Centre for Ecology and Conservation within Exeter’s Penryn Campus in Cornwall.

‘This wasn’t simply a case of fewer species being available – herring, oyster and lobster can all still be bought – but it reflects a genuine narrowing of what readers were being shown and encouraged to cook.’

According to the Marine Stewardship Council, the big five make up 80 per cent of the fish and seafood consumed in the UK. Thurstan said this dominance carried environmental costs: cod, haddock and shrimp fishing, for example, could damage valuable habitats, while salmon farming has come under intense scrutiny.

Thurstan said she had attempted a few of the recipes including ‘Fish baked in custard’ from the 1920s. She said: ‘I tried it with pollack. While the recipe calls it a custard it isn’t sweet, so I think, perhaps with a name change, it has potential.’

Related: Can I get too much protein? Experts answer your questions on the popular supplement

She is also planning to try two 1930s recipes: oyster soup and kipper cream. The latter involves parboiling a kipper and then pounding it with melted butter, lemon juice or vinegar and cayenne until it is the consistency of a cream. ‘I think it would be similar to today’s mackerel pâté, and just as delicious.’

The magazine Thurstan researched was originally published as British Good Housekeeping and is now Good Housekeeping UK. Once published, the paper – entitled ‘Declines in the diversity of fish represented in British domestic recipes over the past 100 years’ – will be published in the journal People and Nature.

January 1923 – Fish baked in custard

‘Purchase a slice of cod or halibut, or some filleted fish weighing about 1lb. Wipe it with a clean cloth and remove any black skin. Lay the fish in a greased and shallow baking-dish and sprinkle it with salt, a little white pepper, the grated rind of half a lemon, and a small onion finely chopped.

‘Then break into a basin 1 or 2 eggs, add 2 tablespoonfuls of flour and a light seasoning of pepper and salt. Beat until smooth and add half pint fresh milk. Strain this custard over the fish, stand the dish in a tin containing some water and bake in a moderate oven until the custard is set and lightly browned (about 30 minutes). It is a good plan to baste the fish once or twice with the custard during the first part of the cooking. Potato chips or some mashed potatoes would be a good accompaniment to this dish.’

May 1934 – Potage aux huîtres

‘One dozen oysters, 1 pint Court bouillon [a broth], 1 pint milk, 1 oz butter, 1 oz flour, 1 tablespoonful cream or unsweetened evaporated milk, seasoning. Oyster soup can be made with tinned oysters or fresh ones. There is no need, however, to buy the choicest variety, as the small ones answer quite well. In no circumstances should oysters be boiled, or they will become hard, leathery and indigestible.’
output.standfirst: Ruth Thurstan studied more than 1,000 Good Housekeeping recipes since 1923 and found whale meat curry and oyster cocktail giving way to five dominant species: cod, haddock, tuna, salmon and prawns
output.progress: Thurstan is testing more historical recipes, including 1930s oyster soup and kipper cream, and submitting her findings to the journal People and Nature.
